title: The Governance Point may not include technical detail it does not itself fully understand
content:
Tucked into the technical-detail guidance, A.1.10.2.4.8.1.4 imposes a duty on the writer rather than the document: "In cases where technical details are included, the Governance Point must ensure they **fully understand the technical aspects themselves** to present them accurately and clearly."

The practice being forbidden is the default one everywhere else: copying a technically correct paragraph from an engineer's forum post into a voter-facing document. That produces text which is accurate but unowned — nobody in the publication chain can answer a question about it, and nobody would notice if it described the wrong module.

Requiring comprehension makes the writer a genuine checkpoint. A description that has been understood and re-expressed by a second party has passed through a comprehension test that copy-paste skips entirely, which is why translation catches errors that proofreading does not.

It also puts a self-limiting brake on the previous rule. If technical content may only be included when the Governance Point understands it, then the volume of technical content is bounded by their actual understanding — so "minimize technical detail" and "understand what you include" reinforce each other instead of competing. The same logic underlies Chesterton's Fence at A.1.10.2.4.7.4.5: no party may wave through something whose reasoning they cannot explain.
description: A.1.10.2.4.8.1.4 bars pass-through of copied technical text, making accurate presentation contingent on the presenter's own comprehension rather than on the source's authority.
